prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose in which memory, the body and dream become an encyclopedic metaphysical project, renewing the novel's imaginative and formal means.

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change after the exchange and the chair's questions: one writer, Mircea Cărtărescu, in one prize part. The ground is the one I gave in round 1. His is a voice I can recognise at the level of the sentence and the whole book, and I do not find the same combination elsewhere on this shortlist. Blinding and Solenoid, as publicly known, build the body, memory and cosmology into a single imaginative architecture. Solenoid comes well after the Orbitor volumes, so the public record at least shows a later large work that extends the project rather than a single early peak. I cannot name further later volumes with enough confidence to build an argument on them, and I say so plainly. I have tested the case against the reservations that colleagues raised, and none of them has displaced the first-place judgment. The unanimous opening placements still count for nothing as merit. Only the criteria carry the case: voice, formal and linguistic ambition, imaginative depth, and sustained quality across a body of work, read within the framework of Nobel's will. On citation scope, I keep the wording anchored in the prose, where my evidence is strongest. I leave out any 'European tradition' framing and any national framing, because those add a claim about lineage that the literary argument does not need. The citation also stays whole-oeuvre in scope without asserting more coverage of the poetry than public translation supports.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that the central claim of linguistic distinctiveness, namely Romanian rhythm, long-sentence control and wordplay, is the part I can least verify. My judgment rests on public knowledge and translation reception, not on independent reading of the originals. The chair's question asks what would count against the claim that the late work deepens the early project. My answer: if Romanian-reading assessments or translators' accounts showed that the later volumes recycle the early images without development, or that quality is concentrated in a few peaks, the whole-oeuvre citation would weaken. In that case I would turn to Murnane (B001) or Yan Lianke (B002), whose cases I find more compact or more uneven but still serious. The maximalist, self-referential scale may also limit breadth of significance. I regard that as a real open question, not a settled flaw. The poetry, early work and essays are covered less well in translation than the major novels, so the oeuvre is judged unevenly.

responses.point: Palm proposes a citation in which poetry is the ground of the prose, and answers the breadth objection by saying that the project's breadth lies in joining the intimate (body, memory, dream) to the encyclopedic, and in reaching across poetry and prose.
responses.response: Her answer on breadth is the strongest reply I have seen to the worry I raised myself, and I find it persuasive as a description of how the project is built. Where I stay more cautious is the citation. I am not able to judge the poetry well enough through translation to name it as the ground of the work, and the chair's question asks us to be exact about what we can stand behind. I would keep the citation on the prose and leave the poetry as context unless a colleague with firmer knowledge of it can show how it carries weight. This is a difference of evidential caution, not of literary judgment. I would not object to a wording that mentions the wider work, provided it does not claim more than the evidence supports.

responses.point: Swärd's citation places the work in a 'European tradition of inward and fantastic narrative', and she says the case must rest on literary form and not on national symbolism or on the circumstances of publication.
responses.response: I share her principle completely and have applied it to Yan Lianke as well: form, not context, must decide. I would still leave the 'European tradition' phrase out of the citation. It is a claim about lineage that needs its own argument, and it risks sliding into the regional or national framing that the chair asked us to avoid. A citation that names what the prose does is more exact and easier to defend. I also take her point that a longer, more continuous corpus supports a whole-oeuvre judgment better than a compact one, and it is part of why Cărtărescu stays ahead of Murnane for me. I would not use that to dismiss Murnane, whose intensity is a legitimate literary quality.

responses.point: Olsson raises, as an open interpretive question, how the will's reference to work of an idealistic tendency applies to an inward, encyclopedic and often disturbing imaginative project, and he declines to treat it as settled either way.
responses.response: I agree that it is open, and I would not settle it by subject matter. A dark or disturbing imaginative world is not in itself a lack of idealism. A project that treats the body, memory and the cosmos as one question about human existence can be read as an ambitious attempt at orientation. My own working account, drawn from my sense of the will rather than from any ruling, is that it asks for a high ideal of literary achievement and a wide human reach. On that reading I do not think the question tells against Cărtărescu, but I accept that it needs a shared reading, and the same reading must then be applied evenly to Carson's ironic and formally radical work. I would not use it to exclude either of them.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Murnane fifth because his deliberately narrow range makes significance across a body of work harder to carry. She places Carson second and treats his case as one of intensity of method rather than extension.
responses.response: She states the difference between the two cases accurately, and I agree with her on the main point: intensity and extension are different kinds of achievement, and the criterion of significance across a body of work favours extension when the voice is otherwise comparable. I ranked Murnane second because his voice and syntax are less exposed to translation loss, so my judgment of him is on firmer ground than my judgment of Cărtărescu's Romanian. That is a point about my evidence, not about relative merit. I differ with her on Carson only in degree. I ranked her sixth because I cannot yet see whether her later work consolidates or restates the early breakthroughs, and I would want the core oeuvre fixed first, as the chair's question suggests.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Adonis second for reshaping Arabic poetic language, and he says that translation is the caveat he would press hardest on his own judgment, asking whether Arabic readers could settle what translation hides.
responses.response: His question applies with equal force to my own judgment of Cărtărescu, and I take it as a fair test of the whole exchange. The asymmetry matters. If the committee accepts translators' accounts and reception as adequate evidence for a prose case, it should apply the same standard to Adonis, and it should not reward a candidate simply because the loss in translation is more visible for poetry. I ranked Adonis fourth. I would keep his poems and his critical prose on poetic language separate from his public role, and I would give age and timing no weight at all, since they are not literary criteria.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's verbal texture, rhythm and long-sentence control in Romanian survives translation; my judgment rests on public knowledge and reception, not on independent reading of the originals.

Whether the later very long novels deepen the early project or extend it without development; I can point to Solenoid as a later large work but cannot verify its quality across its full length or name other later volumes with confidence.
Coverage of the poetry, early work and essays in translation is thinner than for the major novels, so the whole-oeuvre judgment is based unevenly on the novels.
How the will's reference to an idealistic tendency should be read, and whether one shared reading can be applied evenly to Cărtărescu, Carson and others.

For Adonis, Yan Lianke and Michon the decisive stylistic qualities are language-dependent, so my comparisons with them are less secure than my comparison of the prose cases I can approach through translation.
I have not independently verified any of the works or the critical consensus discussed here.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. The supplied profile records no connection to any shortlisted writer. My practice as a novelist and critic of historical and psychological fiction, and my book on Emilie Flygare-Carlén, are context only and not evidence of a preference. My institutional ties to colleagues on the committee, including having joined it together with Swärd, are not connections to any candidate. No recusal is needed.
